source: Helms, Vattam, Goel, Yen, Weissburg (2008) Problem-driven and solution-based design: twin processes of biologically inspired design (ACADIA; precursor of Helms, Vattam & Goel 2009 Design Studies 30(5))
finding: Founding descriptive study of bio-inspired design (BID). Two processes: problem-driven (define problem, reframe in biological terms, search biology, define solution, extract principle, apply) and solution-based (start from a biological solution, extract principle, reframe, search for a problem, apply).
numbers: Georgia Tech course ME/ISyE/MSE/PTFe/BIOL 4803, Fall 2006: 45 students in teams of 4-5 (one biologist per team), 9 projects. 4 of 9 projects (2006) and 5 of 10 (2007 follow-up) were solution-driven. Literature review of 70 cases: solution-driven at least as common as problem-driven.
limits: Observational classroom study, not a lab experiment; no control group; students new to BID; retrospective literature cases are mostly outcome-focused.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of an analogue can start from either end. An agent needs both a problem-to-source path and a source-to-problem path (O7).

source: Helms et al. (2008) same paper: reframing ('biologizing') and search heuristics
finding: Step 2 of problem-driven BID is to restate the problem in biological terms as a question, which becomes the retrieval cue. Instructors gave four search heuristics: change constraints, champion adapters, variation within a solution family, multi-functionality.
numbers: Example reframe: 'stopping a bullet' became 'what characteristics do organisms have that enable them to prevent, withstand and heal damage?'. Example i-Fabric team found 6 biological sources (penguins, wood storks, arctic wolves, beehives, chameleons, humans).
quote: How do biological solutions accomplish xyz function?
limits: Heuristics were taught, not tested against a baseline. No measure of how much reframing improved retrieval.
agent_relevance: Reframe the problem to a function-level, domain-neutral question before retrieval. This is a typed reframe step that code can enforce.

source: Helms et al. (2008) same paper: fixation and structure focus
finding: Teams fixated on the first biological source they met. Alternative sources were dropped at the first difficulty even when the first source had the same difficulty. Solution-driven teams copied structure.
numbers: Fixation shown by abalone-nacre teams (2 of 9 projects, body armor and cell phone case). Structural focus: 100% of solution-driven teams versus 66% of all teams; problem-driven teams focused on function or behaviour 60% of the time. Solution-driven teams always had multi-functional problems; problem-driven 60%. Nacre armor analysis: 100 times too weak, 10 times heavier than Kevlar.
limits: Very small N (9 projects). The later 2021 meta-analysis did not confirm the fixation link (see a06).
agent_relevance: Guard: after the first retrieved analogue, force at least one rival source to be evaluated with the same criteria (anti-fixation).

source: Helms et al. (2008) same paper: compound analogy
finding: Designs often combine several analogues, one per sub-problem; applying an analogy creates new sub-problems that call for new retrievals.
numbers: i-Fabric: phase-change wax from beehive plus counter-current heat bypass from wood stork and arctic wolf. Compound analogical designs in 6 of 9 projects (2006), per the companion paper (Vattam & Goel 2013).
limits: Counts come from the companion paper.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is a loop inside decomposition, not one call. Each subfunction is a separate query.

source: Goel & Hancock (2021) Multifunctional and domain independent? A meta-analysis of case studies of biologically inspired design (Design Science 7, e24)
finding: Re-tested two common assumptions on the Design Study Library. Domain independence is questionable: solution-based design is common in physiology cases, problem-driven in sensing cases. Solution-based design leads to multifunctional designs more often.
numbers: 83 case studies (Georgia Tech 2006-2013), 74 analysed. Multifunctional 36/74 (48.6%). Solution-based 27/74 (36.5%). Two coders, Cohen kappa 0.88 (94% agreement). Assessment 2: multifunctional 22/27 solution-based vs 14/47 problem-driven (81.5% vs 29.8%). Fisher p<0.001, Pearson r=0.662 (solution-based) and -0.374 (problem-driven, p=0.001).
quote: The solution-based process leads to multifunctional designs more often than the problem-driven process.
limits: Students on one course, not practitioners. The authors warn of selection bias and small cells (sensing n=10). Scale independence was not tested.
agent_relevance: A retrieval policy should not be the same for every domain. Route by type of source domain; use solution-first retrieval when many functions are wanted.

source: Goel & Hancock (2021): failed replication of the fixation hypothesis
finding: Earlier hypothesis (Vattam, Helms & Goel 2007; Helms et al. 2009) said solution-based design causes fixation on the biological structure. The new meta-analysis confirmed multifunctionality but found no correlation between solution-based design and structural fixation.
numbers: Fixation tagged in 50/74 cases overall; solution-based 19/27 (70.4%, assessment 2) vs problem-driven 31/47 (66%). Assessment 1: 80% vs 65.6%. Not a significant association. Earlier meta-analysis used 77 cases from the literature.
limits: Authors say it may be an effect of teaching that warned students about fixation. Fixation coding was conservative (structure only).
agent_relevance: Do not treat fixation as a fixed cost of starting from a source. It depends on instruction; a prompt that warns against fixation may be enough.

source: Goel & Hancock (2021): domain pattern details
finding: Physiology cases tended to be solution-based; sensing cases tended to be problem-driven. Compound analogy never co-occurred with solution-based design (r=-1.0).
numbers: Coder 1: 8 of 9 solution-based cases were physiology; coder 2: 7 of 12. Sensing: coder 1 8 of 9 problem-driven, coder 2 7 of 10. Problem-based with compound analogy p=0.008, r=0.316 (coder 1); p=0.001, r=0.374 (coder 2).
limits: Two coders disagree on several cells. Only two domain patterns were tested for significance.
agent_relevance: Compound (multi-source) designs come from problem-driven runs. Use problem-first when the task needs several sub-solutions.

source: Vattam & Goel (2013) Seeking bioinspiration online: a descriptive account (Design Society)
finding: Two in situ studies show that finding a biological analogue is mostly online search and has three difficulties: findability, recognizability, understandability. Designers 'biologize' the problem to bridge the vocabulary gap, but there are no explicit rules.
numbers: Fall 2006: 45 students, 9 teams, observational. Fall 2008: 43 students, 8 teams, one participant-researcher in team FORO (6 people) who collected 39 articles in 7 weeks at 2-3 h per week each: about 3 person-hours per relevant article. 53 false positives logged by the researcher. Compound solutions: 6/9 (66%) in 2006, 4/10 (40%) in 2007.
quote: Finding biological analogies relevant to a design problem is difficult because of the cross-domain nature of the analogies.
limits: Qualitative; one embedded team; false negatives cannot be observed. Students are biology novices.
agent_relevance: Retrieval, not generation, is the bottleneck in BID. Recognition of a good source from a ranked snippet fails often. Add a cheap screening step with explicit criteria before deep reading.

source: Vattam & Goel (2013): theory of analogical retrieval used (ARCS plus information foraging)
finding: Retrieval of analogues is modelled as ARCS (Thagard et al. 1990: three simultaneous constraints, semantic, structural, pragmatic similarity) combined with Information Foraging Theory (Pirolli). Classic models treat retrieval as internal memory; BID retrieval is situated in external information environments.
numbers: ARCS described as three constraints acting at once. MAC/FAC (Forbus, Gentner & Law 1995) and Kolodner's CBR are named as the other base theories.
limits: Description is second-hand for ARCS and MAC/FAC (original papers not opened, see a24 and a25). No test of the combined model is reported here.
agent_relevance: Retrieval should score at least surface, structure and goal relevance together, then use a cheap pass followed by a costly pass (MAC/FAC idea).

source: Goel (2015) Is biologically inspired invention different? (ICCC 2015)
finding: Task model of BID from 83 projects (2006-2013, about 350 students). Claims BID differs from other analogy-based design in five ways: cross-domain by definition, problem-solution co-evolution, problem decomposition drives analogy, compound analogy, interactive analogical retrieval.
numbers: 83 case studies from the ME/ISyE/MSE/BME/BIOL 4740 course, about 350 students. Typical team 4-5 with at least one biology student.
quote: The subfunctions in the functional decomposition of the design problem act as probes into a memory of biological systems.
limits: Position paper built on the author's own corpus. Still lists solution-based fixation as a finding; the 2021 meta-analysis (a06) later undid it.
agent_relevance: Subfunctions of the decomposed problem act as probes into a memory of biological systems: decompose first, retrieve per subfunction.

source: Goel (2015) ICCC: serendipity and design patterns as the unit of transfer
finding: Retrieval is often serendipitous: a team parks a problem, meets an analogue later on another problem, and switches back. Units of transfer are design patterns (domain principles, causal mechanisms, structural arrangements).
numbers: No quantitative result; three kinds of pattern named (domain principles, generic teleological mechanisms, structural arrangements).
limits: Anecdotal evidence for serendipity.
agent_relevance: Keep a parked-problem list and re-test it against every new source found.

source: Goel (2015) AAAI workshop: Biologically inspired design, a new paradigm for AI research on computational sustainability?
finding: Describes tool support for analogue retrieval: AskNature (functionally indexed library), Idea-Inspire and DANE (structured multimodal functional representations), Biologue (semantic annotations of function and causal process on biology articles for retrieval). Process: interactive retrieval online, understand, abstract design patterns, transfer.
numbers: No evaluation numbers in this paper. Data-flow diagram marks places where AI can help.
limits: Overview paper; tool performance not measured here.
agent_relevance: Index sources by function and causal process, not by keyword. This is the structural basis for retrieval by an LLM agent.

source: Helms & Goel (2013) Grounded knowledge representations for biologically inspired design (ICED13): SR.BID
finding: SR.BID extends Structure-Behavior-Function with problem-side categories (operational environment, performance criteria, constraints, perceived deficiencies) so that problem descriptions can be coded and matched to biological analogues.
numbers: Initial coding: 2405 words into 636 concepts, 66 (10.4%) unrelated. Refinement: ~15 weeks, two coders, more than 1000 concepts. Test of 5 random statements: 129 of 147 concepts matched (87.8%), 63 of 72 relations matched (87.2%). Relationship kappa .703 before negotiation. Final set 31 statements, 856 relevant concepts, 2.7% uncoded; operating environment 26.9% of concepts.
limits: Coding scheme built on student problem statements from one course; the vocabulary may not carry over to other design areas.
agent_relevance: Describe the target problem with a fixed slot structure (function, environment, constraints, criteria). Same slots on the source side allow structural matching.

source: Vattam, Helms, Goel (2010) A content account of creative analogies in biologically inspired design (AI EDAM 24(4):467-481)
finding: Single extended design episode analysed with why, what, how, when questions of analogy to build a content theory of creative analogies. Abstract says current BID is ad hoc with little systematisation of biological knowledge or transfer.
numbers: One case; no counts available (only the abstract page could be opened).
limits: Full text not opened (abstract page only); one case only.
agent_relevance: Supports analysing retrieval as a sequence of question types (why use an analogy, what to take, how, when).

source: Goel, Bras, Helms, Rugaber, Tovey, Vattam, Weissburg, Wiltgen, Yen (2011) Design patterns and cross-domain analogies in biologically inspired sustainable design (AAAI Spring Symposium)
finding: Corpus analysis of 42 designs for sustainability; fog-harvesting net case yields two function-mechanism design patterns (Hydrophobia, Hydrophilia) that recur across projects. Argues design patterns are the unit of cross-domain transfer.
numbers: Corpus 42 designs: 26 appeared sustainable (20 intended, 6 incidental). Authors call the share unreliable because two semesters asked for sustainability.
limits: Selection effect from course assignment; pattern analysis is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Store retrieved sources as reusable function-mechanism patterns, not as whole stories.

source: Hashemi Farzaneh (2020) Bioinspired design: impact of collaboration between engineers and biologists on analogical transfer and ideation (Res Eng Des 31:299-322)
finding: Lab experiment on pairs. Ideas that contain correct or incomplete analogies, true analogies and organ or state-change transfer scored higher in quality than other bio-inspired ideas, which scored higher than non-biological ideas. Supported engineer-biologist pairs transferred more correct analogies than single-discipline pairs.
numbers: 20 doctoral candidates (10 biologists, 10 mechanical engineers), 20 pairs (5 each: biologist, engineer, engineer-biologist, supported engineer-biologist), 196 ideas (187 at working-principle level). Mean task-specific quality: about 60% selected analogy categories, about 50% other bio-inspired, about 40% not bio-inspired. ANOVA F=8.30, 8.44, 8.27, critical 3.04, p about 0.0003, df=193. Supported pairs vs single-discipline: p<0.2% on accuracy of documented ideas.
limits: Five pairs per condition; unsupported collaboration was not significant on all ideas (p>10%). Same participants worked in both pair types, so samples are not independent. Inter-coder agreement 71-84%.
agent_relevance: Quality rises when the transfer is of mechanism type and accurate, so the agent should check what part of the mechanism holds in the target before building on it. A structured template helps (BioId Support).

source: Hashemi Farzaneh (2020): effect of the BioId Support template
finding: A two-step support (describe biological information at low abstraction, then abstract and transfer, with sketch and graph templates, one template per source) raised the share of correct and incomplete analogies that were transferred.
numbers: Support pairs highest on all three analogy categories. Documented ideas: significantly higher accuracy at p<0.2%, similarity p<1%, element of transfer p<10%. Participants had no prior bio-inspired design experience.
limits: Wilcoxon rank-sum with n=5 pairs per group; alpha 10% used for some claims.
agent_relevance: A fixed two-step scaffold (concrete description, then abstraction) is a tested way to improve transfer quality. Supports O7 as a template.

source: Dekel, Burns, Goldwater (2021 preprint) Leaping across the mental canyon: higher-order long-distance analogical retrieval
finding: Replicates the late analogical abstraction effect of Gentner et al. (2009): comparing two analogous cases at the time of use makes a past analogous case more likely to be retrieved. Extends it to cross-domain cues (letter-strings to stories). Retrieval of higher-order relational matches is possible but rare.
numbers: Exp 1: 125 undergraduates; story cues, surface 13/21 (61.9%) vs 5/43 (11.6%); higher-order 5/42 (11.9%) in the contrast group, chi2(1,N=64)=7.107, p=.008, phi=.33. Letter-string cues Exp 1: higher-order 4/20 (20%) vs 4/40 (10%), p=.283, not significant. Exp 2 (N=239): higher-order story retrieved 22/59 (37.3%) vs 13/120 (10.8%), p<.001. Exp 3 (N=121, longer delay, more distractors): 7/35 (20.0%) vs 4/86 (4.7%), p=.008. Pooled: 53/174 (30.5%) vs 21/246 (8.5%), phi=.28.
quote: Participants that explicitly compared target cases were significantly more likely to retrieve the relevant source case than participants that did not compare them.
limits: Preprint (not peer reviewed in this version). Undergraduates, online, small story set. Surface and first-order effects inconsistent in Exp 3. Authors say effects may be mapping not retrieval.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by deep structure works only after an explicit comparison and abstraction of the principle. For an agent, abstract a schema from the current problem first and use that as the retrieval cue; raw surface description retrieves surface matches.

source: Dekel et al. (2021): surface similarity dominates retrieval
finding: Across experiments, a surface-level schema cue retrieved the surface-matched story more often than any relational cue. In the hardest condition (Exp 3) surface and first-order effects vanished while the higher-order effect remained.
numbers: Surface-schema retrieval Exp 2: 51/59 (86.4%) vs 64/180 (35.6%); Exp 3: 13/40 (32.5%) vs 23/81 (28.4%), p=.642. Overall chi2 in Exp 3 not significant (chi2(6,N=121)=10.811, p=.094).
limits: Same limits as a18. Differences between experiments are not fully explained by the authors.
agent_relevance: Expect an LLM, like people, to retrieve surface-similar sources first; deliberately add a structural rewrite of the query.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design (J Mech Des 133(8))
finding: Experiment crossing analogical distance (near vs far field), commonness (more vs less common) and modality (picture vs text) of patent examples. Far-field, less-common examples raised novelty and variability in quality. Effects not modulated by modality.
numbers: Senior engineering students; examples from US Patent database; control group with no examples. Far-field plus less-common examples gave more novel concepts than control. (Abstract only; sample sizes not read.)
limits: Abstract only via Crossref. Full text was behind a paywall.
agent_relevance: Far analogies help novelty but not reliably quality. Choose distance by goal: novelty or feasibility.

source: Fu, Chan, Cagan, Kotovsky, Schunn, Wood (2013) The meaning of near and far (J Mech Des 135(2):021007)
finding: Second study using patents structured by latent semantic analysis and a Bayesian structural-form algorithm. Findings looked contradictory to the 2011 study until all stimuli were mapped into one structure: near and far are relative to the problem, not absolute.
numbers: Abstract only: no N or effect sizes read.
limits: Abstract only via Crossref. Reported as partly conflicting with Chan et al. 2011 until relative distance was modelled.
agent_relevance: Distance is relative to the target problem. Compute distance per query (for example embedding distance) rather than label sources near or far in general.

source: Linsey, Wood, Markman (2012) Design by analogy: a study of the WordTree method for problem re-representation (J Mech Des 134(4)); 2008 conference version
finding: WordTree method: re-represent the problem as verbs and walk word hierarchies to find far-domain analogies without special databases. Controlled experiment and redesign projects: users found significantly more analogies and searched outside the problem domain compared with control.
numbers: Abstract only. Examples: a cherry pitter implemented for a peanut sheller; dump truck and gold panning for a cat litter box.
limits: Abstract only via Crossref; sample sizes and effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: A typed re-representation step (problem to verb hierarchy, then synonyms and hypernyms) is a published way to widen the search space. Fits O4/O8 as a code-driven reframe.

source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure (Memory & Cognition 35:29-38)
finding: Analysis of real engineering design activity: title says it links analogical distance to the function of the analogy and to preinventive structures. Details not read.
numbers: Not read: no numbers recorded.
limits: Paywalled; only title and bibliographic record available. Not to be cited for numbers.
agent_relevance: Flag as a source to read in angle B or by the parent.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1995) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval (Cognitive Science 19:141-205)
finding: Two-stage retrieval model: a cheap content-vector scan (MAC) picks candidates, then a structure-mapping engine (FAC) scores the candidates. Described in Vattam & Goel as a base theory of analogical retrieval.
numbers: Not read in the original; no numbers recorded.
limits: Original not opened; PDF hosts returned errors. Cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an LLM agent: embedding search first (cheap), then a structured critique of structural fit (costly).

source: Thagard, Holyoak, Nelson, Gochfeld (1990) Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction (Artificial Intelligence 46:259-310)
finding: ARCS: retrieval as constraint satisfaction over semantic, structural and pragmatic similarity at once. Described second-hand in Vattam & Goel (2013).
numbers: Not read in the original; no numbers recorded.
limits: Original not opened. Cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: The pragmatic constraint (goal relevance) separates retrieval for design from generic similarity search.

source: Helms, Vattam, Goel (2009) Biologically inspired design: process and products (Design Studies 30(5):606-622)
finding: Journal version of the twin-process finding. Content known through the 2008 ACADIA precursor (a01-a04) and through later citations; the journal text itself was not opened.
numbers: Details taken from the precursor; no new numbers.
limits: Journal text not opened; the search tool returned only bibliographic data.
agent_relevance: Use the 2008 precursor numbers, not claims attributed to the journal paper.

source: Goel & Shu (2015) Analogical thinking: an introduction in the context of design (AI EDAM special-issue editorial)
finding: One-page editorial. Frames the special issue around analogy in the cognitive, external and social worlds, naming experiments on external representation (CAD, photographs, sketches) and on analogizing in teams.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Only an editorial; no data.
agent_relevance: Little direct use; confirms that representation modality of the source is an active research variable.
